utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in court today. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the OTP, to all those in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with assistant Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Mundis. Mr. Mundis -- Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, can you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Safet Sivro.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to speak closer to the microphone. We can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Safet Sivro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, Mr. Sivro, and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of June, 1958, in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in which country is Poculica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Poculica is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivro. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivro, were you ever a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, from the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And were you ever a member of the Command Staff of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the 3rd Corps of the Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you identify the position or positions that you held in the 3rd Corps Command Staff and the time period or periods in which you occupied those positions?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: From late April 1994, I was in the Staff of the 3rd Corps, in the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to repeat the latter part of his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, the witnesses can't -- I beg your pardon. The interpreters are not able to hear you. Could you please speak a little louder and try to speak directly to your microphone so that they can hear you. And will you please repeat the answer you just gave, because they didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: In late April 1994, I came to the Command of the 3rd Corps, where I was assigned to work in the Operations Centre of the Staff and in the Department for Planning and Observing Combat Activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sivro, when you came to the Operations Centre, what was role, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I was a desk officer in the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've referred to the Operations Centre. Within which department of the 3rd Corps Command Staff is the Operations Centre situated?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The Operations Centre is in the Staff of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But is it in a particular department within the 3rd Corps Command Staff or is it not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It forms a constituent part of the Staff. The Operations Centre had its office where the chief of the Operations Centre was located as well as I, and a special part of the Operations Centre was an office where the duty officer was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, are you familiar with the Department for Operations and Training within the 3rd Corps Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: In the Staff of the 3rd Corps, we didn't have a Department for Operations. Rather, we had an Operations and Training Department or Section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was the Operations and Training Department comprised of individual units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It was the constituent part of the Staff or the headquarters which functioned in different sections. One was the Operations Department, another one was training, and the third one was monitoring of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And these different sections that you've referred to, were they all underneath the Operations and Training Department?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No. The Training and Education Section was a separate unit in the Staff of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. Mr. Sivro, going back to -- you'd mentioned that you were a desk officer. Can you -- in the Operations Centre. Can you explain what your responsibilities in that position were?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: For the most part, I received reports from subordinate units. That was the gist of our job. We produced daily orders of the commander for duty shifts and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sivro. And, Mr. Sivro, when you joined the 3rd Corps Command Staff, I believe you mentioned it was late April of 1994, who was the commander of the 3rd Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Sakib Mahmuljin was the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask now that the witness now be shown Exhibit P02464.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To what kind of document would this page belong?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the logbook of daily orders of the IKM, that's to say the forward command post of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could just move on to page number 2 of the English and B/C/S. Mr. Sivro, do you see the initials "SS" on this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To whom do those initials belong?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: These are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why do your initials appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Because I drafted this, I wrote this. I'm the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to section 1(a) of this document. What does that section provide for?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: On the 26th of August, 1995, duty operations officer shall be Major Mensur Brkic and his assistant shall be Lieutenant Suad Grcic. That means the duty officer on that day would be the above-mentioned major, and his assistant was to be the person mentioned there on that date in the Staff of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sivro. What were the responsibilities of a duty operations officer? Are you familiar with those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The duty officer was charged with providing security to the IKM, to maintain the premises, and was responsible for receiving orders from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And there's a reference to an assistant. What would the role of the assistant be?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The role of the assistant was to step in for the duty officer when he was asleep. The duty officer was on duty until 2400 hours, and then he was replaced by his assistant, who would be on duty for the night until 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how were people selected for the duty officer position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The duty officer's highest rank was captain, whereas the assistant duty officers were of lower rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for how long would a person be assigned to the duty officer position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The duty officer was on duty for 24-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. Mr. Sivro, in response to a question that I put to you in terms of how people were selected for the duty officer position, you said that the duty officer's highest rank was captain. I'd refer you to the page in front of you. It appears that the person assigned as the duty officer on the 26th of August, 1995, was a major. Can you clarify your answer, in light of -- in light of the passage that I've just referred you to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. I said that the duty officer was the rank of a captain and above, whereas assistant duty officers were officers holding lower ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Sivro. Were you ever assigned as the duty officer -- duty operations officer? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would ask that this exhibit be tendered into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02463, and I also have the original of that document, and so perhaps it would be best if we pull up the electronic version of that document, but at the same time if the witness could refer to the original hard-copy version of the document which I have in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. If I may ask that should the Prosecutor ask that the document be tendered, for the document to be admitted after my cross-examination. I don't want to go into extensive explanations before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's -- that's fine with me. I'd still like to lay the foundation for admitting the document, and so I'll go through it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I'd just like to refer you to the front -- front of that page, and there should be a reference number on the top of it. It's 01855061. Can you tell me what kind of -- you've got a diary in your hand -- what kind of diary this is, or booklet?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the operations diary of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what's the purpose of this particular diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The purpose of this diary is for the duty officers to make note of the most important events taking part during his duty shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And just for clarification, who's primarily responsible for maintaining this particular diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Those responsible for maintaining the diary or, rather, the person responsible was the duty officers -- the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you could -- if you could turn to the first page in that -- in the diary, Mr. Sivro. It's got a reference number 01855061, and on the e-court version it's page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. Have you found the reference -- the page with the reference 01855061, Mr. Sivro? Excuse me, 5062, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you describe what's set out on this page?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the instruction for keeping an operations diary, providing for the way in which the duty operations officer is to keep the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And there's a reference to -- there's an "F" on the upper right-hand corner of the document, of the page in front of you. What is -- what does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Farz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could just go to page 2 -- the following page of the English, so I guess that would be page 3 of the English, leave it on the same B/C/S page in the screen. Mr. Sivro, if you keep looking at that same document, there are initials "SS" at the bottom left-hand corner of the document. To whom to those initials belong?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: These are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why do your initials appear on this page?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Because I'm the author of the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to page 20 of the B/C/S and English version -- excuse me. The English translation is going to be on ETO1855080. It's page 20 of the e-court B/C/S. And, Mr. Sivro, if you could find the page with the reference 01855080.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Have you found --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd refer you to the entry marked as "309". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, above that entry there are some markings. Can you explain what the significance of those markings are?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't understand. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm referring to -- there's a signature there, two signatures above that entry, and then there are two statements, "Duty handed over by" and "Duty received by." If you could just explain the significance of those markings.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This means that Major Halilagic transferred his duty to Captain Mrkaljevic who took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And took over in what position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The duty officer's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, if I could refer to you entry number 309, whose signature would appear beside that entry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Under "309", I can't say whose signature that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. Thanks. Now, if we could move on to page 8 of the B/C/S, and the English is going to be 01855068.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sivro, if you could find also in the book in front of you the reference -- or the page with the reference 01855068.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could refer you to entry number 70, Mr. Sivro. Do you recognise the signature beside that entry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom does that signature belong?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Mine, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I just have a clarification question for you. Why is it that your signature appears beside the first three entries and it would seem that these entries relate to the date of the 1st of September, 1995, and that another signature appears for the remaining entries for that particular day?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Probably I was stepping in for the duty operations officer at the time, whether he was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: He must have -- I must have been replacing him at the time in the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, that's all I have for the witness on this particular document. Obviously, I won't be tendering it now, but following the Defence's cross-examination we would like to tender this into evidence at that point. So for now, I'd just ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence as marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 511 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'd ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02465 [Realtime transcript read in error "P04265"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it P02465 or P04265?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's 2465 [Realtime transcript read in error"4265"], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I just saw that the transcript was showing a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript still shows the wrong number. It's 2465, not 4265.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, what type of document is this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the war diary of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this particular diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why is it that you're familiar with this particular diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I believe that I kept some war diaries of the 3rd Corps at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you keep this particular diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I would have to look at the contents to be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll look at the contents in just a second. But before we do, I just have one further question for you. Generally, what was the purpose of a war diary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The purpose of a war diary was to set out in it the most important elements of the events of the day in the Staff of the 3rd Corps, in the subordinate units, whether there were any combat activities or not, and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could just move to page 15 of the B/C/S and English now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, there are two entries on this particular -- on the page in front of you. I would refer you to the upper entry. Did you make that entry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would like to refer you to the third bullet point, and the sentence begins: "The commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment," and there's a reference there to "IKM 1". Can you tell us what IKM 1 is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly IKM 1 and 2. There were IKM Klek and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- another one The interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Probably this one is the IKM Klek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you -- you referred to two IKMs and the interpreter didn't hear what the second IKM was. Can you repeat the names of the two IKMs that you just referred to, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: One was IKM Luke, the other one was IKM Klek. And the elevation point was triple 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what did triple 7 relate to, to which IKM?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I assume that it was the IKM 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the function of the IKM Klek?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: At IKM Klek, we were up there, a number of officers, before the beginning of the Farz operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could move on to page 17 of the B/C/S and English. If we could scroll to the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, were you responsible for making this particular entry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And now I'd refer you to the last four lines of the page, and it's the same for the English, it's the last four lines of the English version as well. And I believe there's a -- I'm just going to have the witness read that out, because I believe there's a slight translation error. So for the benefit of the record, I'll just have the witness read out the last four lines. Mr. Sivro, could you read out the last four lines of the text, and it begins -- the sentence, I think, begins with: "During the day ..."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "During the day, the IKM of the 3rd Corps, 1777, was visited by commander of Visoko, Mr. Halid Cengic and Brigadier General Rasid Zorlak."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would just ask that we be allowed to submit a revised translation specific to this particular text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you're saying, Mr. Menon. What do you mean, provide a revised translation specific to this particular text?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, the text that the witness read out, there's a slight translation error on the English version. It refers to an IKM 3, and it's lacking the word "was," actually, so it's more a grammatical error. Obviously, this is just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber doesn't see any utility in it, then we obviously won't do it, but just to make the language as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I hear that, we will probably do that, Mr. Menon, but I see that on the translation that we have just been given now, there doesn't seem to be mention of the person called Commander Halid Cengic. Is that also a correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Are you referring to the translation that the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The translation on the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: On the transcript, I actual -- I see one. I do see the reference to Halid Cengic. It's at line -- it begins at line 24, actually, 14.24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I see here at page 14, line 21, it says: "During the day, the IKM of the 3rd Corps, 1777, was visited by the commander in Visoko" -- oh, Halid Cengic. I beg your pardon. Sorry. And GLOC, what's become of GLOC, Visoko GLOC?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I think -- I mean I can certainly have the witness clarify that, but I think he was obviously elaborating on the word "GLOC." But I could have him clarify that for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, what does "GLOC" refer to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Major Logistical Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Sivro, what positions did Rasid Zorlak and Halid Cengic occupy within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This first one was the commander of the GLOC, and the second one was the Brigadier General Rasid Zorlak who was in the ABHO, something in that sense, the atomic, biological, chemical weapons. He was probably the chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was just looking at me, and I noticed the translation into Bosnian, we are not getting at this moment. There is something wrong. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like we're not getting translations from the Bosnian booth. Was there a problem there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now, it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a problem, but right now we are getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you recall whether Mr. Zorlak and Mr. Cengic visited anybody from the 3rd Corps Command during this particular visit that's referred to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: They were with Commander Sakib --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What was the last name of the person that you just referred to, Mr. Sivro? The interpreter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Commander Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be -- this exhibit be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May the please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit number 512.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02649, 02649.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There's a reference to Postojna. Do you see that on the left-hand column? Does that assist you in understanding what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question? I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There's a reference to Postojna on the left-hand column, and I was wondering whether that would help you in recollecting what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It should be the operations diary, but it doesn't look like an operations diary. It hasn't been done the way it should be. Columns 3 and 4 -- actually, column 3 should say that it was operations, but it should not state who it's from. Actually, it should say who the report was received from, and at the bottom it should say who received it, but from here you can't really see that. It looks like something that could be an operations war diary, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that this document be marked for identification. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI 513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02648.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you know what type of document this is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is a regular combat -- a daily -- a regular daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7 of the English version of this document and page 3 of the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the initials "SS" on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To whom do those initials belong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you repeat yourself, please, Mr. Sivro. The interpreters didn't hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: If this is a regular combat report, these are my initials, "SS," but there were other officers who were on duty and who also had the initials SS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, while you were at the Operations Centre, did you have the responsibility of preparing regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Only if I was the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 1 of the B/C/S and English again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I would note for the record that this document is dated the 22nd of September, 1995. Were you responsible for preparing this particular document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, if I was the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could go to page 4 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I would refer you to the section -- if we could scroll down a little bit on the English version, just a little bit. Thank you. Do you see the section marked "37th dKoV"? Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you could just read to yourself the sentence immediately above that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would be very good if the witness were to read this sentence out loud instead of silently, because I actually see a very wrong translation of this sentence. So perhaps the witness could read it out loud, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, if you could read that sentence out loud.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "Units and commands of the 34th Corps --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot see where the witness is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He's reading from the sentence immediately above the section marked as "37th dKoV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, could you re-read that sentence again?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "Units and commands of the 3rd Corps today during the day were visited by commander of the GSS and ARBiH, General Rasim Delic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, and I don't want you to speculate on this, I only want you to tell me if you know, but do you know which units and commanders Mr. Delic visited that day?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just understand? I thought the witness was asked to read the writing under the heading "37th dKoV," but it looks like he read the writing above "37th dKoV."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Perhaps I misspoke, Your Honour, but that was my intention, to have him read the sentence above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps I misread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if just we can keep the note that the document needs to be corrected. Instead of the words "were visited," the words here are "were inspected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the interpretation by the witness said "visited."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We note that. Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02662.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of document this is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It's an analysis of the combat readiness of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of these -- of this analysis document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The purpose was to compile an analysis at the end of the month and to present it to the higher command about the state of the units of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "higher command," which -- can you be a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The Army General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to page 14 of the English and page 27 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the initials "NP" on the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom to those initials belong?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Nermin Pesto from the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Pesto's position within the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And so in that case he would be your superior, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: For a time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have a role in preparing documents such as this one?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you did have a role in preparing these analysis documents, can you describe how you would go about carrying out that role?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I would compile reports from subordinate units and from sections within the 3rd Corps, and then I would put them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 515.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit P02690. While the English is coming up:

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. What type of document is this, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It's an analysis of the implementation of the monthly plan for -- for the whole year, actually, specifically here for September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain what the purpose of a document like this would be?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The purpose of a document like this would be to make an analysis of the implementation of the monthly plan for a specific month, meaning what the organs within the 3rd Corps did and to see how many tasks were resolved in the course of that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify one point. Would this document relate to the monthly plan of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, the monthly plan of the organs and sections of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 20 of the B/C/S and page 35 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, the document appears to be signed by -- and it hasn't come up on the English as yet, but now it has. The document appears to be signed by Haso Ribo. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, the signature is of Haso Ribo, and the document was signed by Nermin Pesto, because he's the one who drafted this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please understand the previous answer. It says at page 24, line 4: "Yes, the signature is of Haso Ribo, and the document was signed by Nermin Pesto."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, you referred to the document being signed by Nermin Pesto. Was this document -- is the document in front of you signed by Mr. Pesto?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where does Mr. Pesto's signature appear?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It's signed for Haso Ribo. Where it says "for the head of the Department for Operations and Training, Haso Ribo," the document was actually signed for him by Pesto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, the position -- the document states that Mr. Ribo was the head of the Department for Operations and Training. What was the relation -- what was the functional relationship between the Operations Centre and the Department for Operations and Training?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Haso Ribo was the deputy chief of the Staff for Operations and Training. He was not -- he was the assistant chief for Operations and Training, but as part of that there was an operation centre for the monitoring of combat activities and for the planning of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So was the Operations Centre within the Department of Operations and Training?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you worked within the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, for a while I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And now back to this document. Would you have a role in preparing documents such as this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I did that, sometimes Pesto did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain what your role would be?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Our role at the time was to compile, from the other sections and departments, reports on the implementation of the monthly training plan. We would put all of that together and we would send it to the headquarters or the commander for them to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the commander of what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Mostly to the chief of Staff, but sometimes the Corps Commander also would take a copy and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you're referring to the 3rd Corps commander, are you not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P06166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would it be too much to ask you if eventually you will give us a clue as to the purpose of showing these documents to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It would be very helpful. That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I mean, with the time constraints obviously on this particular examination, it hadn't been my plan to go through the particular substance of this document with this witness, but certainly the substance of this document contains information which has either been discussed in other -- by other witnesses or will be discussed by future witnesses. And so at this point I did not plan on going through the substance of this document with this witness. Obviously, to the extent that -- if it were the case that the substance of this document was never discussed by any witness, then that would obviously go to the weight of the document, the weight that the Trial Chamber would attribute to the document. But in terms of my plan for this specific -- for this specific witness, I hadn't planned on discussing the contents of this document with him, but merely to identify it and have him describe what exactly it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, bear in mind then, please, that if you are under time pressure, then you should consider not bringing documents to the witnesses of which the Chamber will have no use, because unless you are sure that there is something substantial in the document that you want the Chamber to be notified or to see or to take into account, then I don't think you should waste your time in bringing it to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly didn't intend to try and have a document admitted that would never be discussed by a witness. My -- the only point that I was making was simply that it is certainly my expectation that the contents of this document will be discussed by a future witness and that the contents of -- certainly some aspects of this document have been discussed by other witnesses. I mean, the witness -- this witness has identified this document as a summary of work performed by 3rd Corps departments and units, and so we've already had testimony relating to the operation of the 3rd Corps in this particular time period. And so that's why -- and that is part of the reason why I thought it sufficient to have this document admitted, without getting this particular witness's explanation of the substantive content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But I would then suggest that you wait to bring the document before the witness until you do it in front of the witness who will actually testify to its substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do, because it's very confusing for us, not knowing what the documents are intended to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that, Your Honour. I will keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I rose to my feet at the point when His Honour Judge Harhoff started speaking. I was just about to raise my objection, and I didn't manage to before it was admitted. If the Prosecutor could attempt to link up the documents and the witnesses through which the documents are admitted, because we don't really see why Mr. Sivro is testifying to this document rather than the witness who will be taking the stand tomorrow and whose signature is on this document. And my same objection applies to all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're up, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hate to rise to my feet when one of my colleagues is leading a witness, but let me again simply indicate that what we're trying to do is bring in witnesses who can authenticate documents, the contents of which have either been the subject of prior testimony or will be the subject of subsequent testimony. With all due respect, it seems as though the Prosecution is in a bit of a situation where we're between a rock and a hard place. We could -- we could take the approach of trying to tender documents without any witness to testify about them. That is in many instances problematic. What we're simply trying to do is have the person who dealt with this document, in many instances wrote the entries in the document, come in and explain that and serve as a conduit through which the logbooks or other documents can be admitted into evidence, with the full expectation either that prior witnesses have testified as to the contents or future witnesses will testify about the contents. When we have logbooks -- when certain witnesses have produced them and other witnesses who can talk about the contents, it's our view that we need both of those witnesses in order to get both the logbook in and for the Chamber to hear about the actual contents of the documents, and that's simply all we're trying to do. If we need to bring witnesses in to do that, then unfortunately that's what we have to do. We've tried doing a similar exercise through Rule 92 ter. That was rejected by the Trial Chamber. We're simply trying to get a situation where the logbooks come in and we have witnesses who can talk about the contents of what's in the logbooks. Those are not always one and the same person, and that's simply what we're trying to do with this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the specific point raised by Madam Vidovic, that this witness is now being used to tender a document that appears to have been authored by Nermin Pesto, who is yet to be called? And the question really is: Why couldn't this document wait for Nermin Pesto to come and be tendered through him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, Nermin Pesto, we expect to testify, is listed also for one hour. There are a large number of documents that we will be seeking to tender and admit into evidence by way of that witness. What we're trying to do is move as expeditiously as possible with the witnesses we have, in the time available, given the large number of documents that we believe Your Honours need in order to fully assess this case. Similarly, with respect, for example, to the logbooks, there are numerous persons whose names and initials appear in those documents. We're not in a position to call all of those witnesses. We're simply trying to link the exhibits through witnesses who can testify as to their authenticity and the way in which they were produced. It's easy to find a certain example here or there where we could have selected a different witness to testify about those documents, but clearly what we're trying to do, with the limited time that we have available, is to get these documents that we believe are relevant and have a certain degree of probative value before Your Honours so that you have all the evidence that you need to reach the conclusions that you must at the end of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Did you tender the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I asked that it be tendered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you see the picture in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody on this picture?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would just ask if the usher could assist the witness. I'm going to have him make some markings on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us whom you recognise on this particular -- on the picture?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The late President Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Any other people?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Commander Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking us to make markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I will, once he's mentioned the names, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to go back again to say, "Okay, mark so-and-so," "Mark so-and-so"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I take your point. I'll ask him to mark as he goes along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, you've mentioned Mr. Izetbegovic. Can you place a "1" on Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Here [marks]?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Shall I write 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: 2 is Commander Sakib Mahmuljin. 3 is Colonel Ribo, Haso. 4 is Fadil Hasanagic [Realtime transcript read in error "father"].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone else on that picture?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'm just -- I'm looking at the transcript, and it says "4 is Father."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, who did you mark with the number 4?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02466 [Realtime transcript read in error "P04266"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P02466, not 4266. 2466, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar informs me that the markings for Exhibit 517 have been lost. Could we mark them again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, could you mark the people that you've just referred to, and mark them with the same numbers. And as you go along, please repeat the names that you've -- that you've marked and the numbers that you've marked.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Number 1 is the state president late Alija Izetbegovic. 2 is the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin. Number 3 is Colonel Haso Ribo, and number 4 is Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could capture that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we've got it now. We can go to P02466. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could bring up P02466 on the screen, please. If we could just go to -- if we could go to page 3 of the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, what type of document -- what type of document is this, the one that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the mail delivery or dispatch logbook of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who within the 3rd Corps was responsible for maintaining this particular dispatch delivery book, as you referred to it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The headquarters administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And how would the documents listed in this particular booklet have been sent to their recipients?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: As for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, you need to speak up. The interpreters didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This was sent by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02417, 2417.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I would like you to just take a look at the page in front of you, and then if we could move to page 15 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. And now if we could move to page 16 of the -- can we get the whole B/C/S page onto this screen? Do you see that page in front of you, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Look at page 16 of the B/C/S and stay on the same page in English. Do you see that in front of you, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do, but not clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on it a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you know what type of -- what type of documents this is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would simply ask that this document be marked for identification, Your Honour, and I'm finished with this witness. This particular document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is going to be dealt with by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: This is a register of mail, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said that brings you to the conclusion of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess that's a convenient time to take the break. Can we take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sivro. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and today I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence for General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since both of us speak the same language, I urge you to make a small break before answering my question and to speak up, please, because the interpreters had difficulty hearing you. You will be able to answer most of my questions with a yes or no. However, if you feel that you need to provide an explanation, since I think that your testimony can help a great deal in clarifying matters, I ask you and invite you to provide an explanation, if you feel you have to or if the Trial Chamber calls upon you to do so. Mr. Sivro, would you tell the Trial Chamber what sort of schools you completed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I completed the technical/chemical high school, and then I completed a further two years of higher schooling, which was common under the Yugoslav system at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have no military education whatsoever; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I completed a course for squad leader in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I am right, am I not, in saying that before performing the duties of the chief of staff of the brigade or, rather, the operations officer, you had not been trained for these duties at all?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I was not, I had not been.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not attend any courses or training enabling you to handle information of military character in a proper manner, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said not in the course of the war, but let me ask you this: You did not complete the relevant schools for that sort of duty, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is true, is it not, that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout the war, did not have schooled officers of the sort, and you had to accept this job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in your work in the Operations Centre, that's to say in the planning section. Before I move on to that, let us clarify one matter. In your evidence, you stated that you were not the only person who, in the course of 1995, was on the roster of operations duty officers in the Command of the 3rd Corps, bearing the initials "SS."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. There were two more officers who had the same initials as I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. These were Senad Selimovic and Sead Sejman [phoen]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, when we see the initials "SS," this does not necessarily mean that you provided the documentation or that you drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, if it concerns the Staff, if it concerns documents from the Operations Centre and documents concerning combat readiness, then they must be mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this refers to the Operations Centre documents?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Witness, you're asked to repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put the question to you again. Perhaps it's easier this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the document concerning Operations Centre bear the initials SS, this means that you produced them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the gist of the answer you gave a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, I worked also in the combat activities section, so there are documents I produced there, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak slowly and enunciate more clearly, because I didn't even understand you in Bosnian. Can you please repeat your answer slowly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I worked in the Staff of the 3rd Corps, in the Operations Centre for a while and in the section for planning and monitoring combat activities, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this is the Section for Planning and Monitoring Combat Activities, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, and if my initials appeared there in such documents, too, then it means I drafted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, very well. Let us clarify matters further. In the Section for Planning and Monitoring Combat Activities, if I understood you well, you worked there starting from April 1994. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: From April 1994 through to the end of the war, I changed sections, and I can't really give you specific time limits. I know that for a while I worked in the Operations Centre, and for a while I worked in the planning and monitoring of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, my understanding of your evidence is that you were acting as duty officer only occasionally. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only twice monthly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Twice monthly, perhaps more often if needed, but that was the average.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the documents you saw and the documents you were shown by the Prosecutor today, you can only comment upon the information contained therein if you were the one presenting the documents in drafting them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, only if I included them in these documents, if I entered them in these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I just didn't understand what you were saying, Madam Interpreter. You say, "If you were the one presenting the documents in drafting them." I don't understand what that means. And when you say "only if I included them in these documents," I didn't understand what that means. It doesn't seem to answer the question put.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter meant "only if I entered the information in the documents as I was drafting them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's much better. Thank you so much. You may proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your testimony today, you touched upon the question of forward command posts. They are mentioned in the documents, aren't they, specifically in document presented to you by the Prosecutor today, the operations logbook of the IKM, the forward command post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber how many forward command posts the 3rd Corps had during the Farz operation in September 1995, if you recall all of them?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: There was an IKM at Luke. Then there was an IKM at Klek, at elevation 777. There was a forward command post at Stavci and another one in Trepca. There was another one in Maglaj at Natron.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will just clarify for the transcription. You mentioned the IKM, Luke, then Klek, then Stavci, Natron and Trepca. Very well. Also, there were observations posts for the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, there was an observation post of the 3rd Corps at the time of the operation, and it was at the triple 7 location, the Klek. That was the observation post of the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that. All right. Now, what I want to ask you is the following: All the command posts functioned at a specific time period, let's say, of a month; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: More or less for about a month, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that telephone connections at that time were not constantly working; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: We used induction telephones.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the field telephone?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that when you were working in the Operations Centre, reports were reaching you which contained incorrect data as well; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say whether the data was correct or incorrect. If I read a regular report, of course it was possible that there was some inaccuracies or untruths there or that unit commanders were exaggerating things in the report and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in August 1995, a thematic briefing was held in the morale and personnel section of the 3rd Corps, attended in person by Commander Delic, and he pointed to the problem of false information; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. Thank you. I will ask you something else. From what I understand of your testimony, you said that you received reports at the Operations Centre from subordinate commands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you summarised those reports into one report, and then you would forward that to the superior command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about reports by the 3rd Corps, would you agree that they were always drafted in segments; for example, for morale, aggressor forces, our forces, morale, logistics, Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's how the reports were drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that those parts of the report were done by the assistant commander for that section, each dealing with their own topic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. The assistant for morale, logistics, legal affairs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is for the Trial Chamber to understand how this worked. So as part of the 3rd Corps, the assistant for morale would summarise the information that had to do with morale, and then the assistant for military security would do that for the security part, and then you would put all of those topics together into one report; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm correct, am I not, if I say that there was a duty shift logbook which recorded each day exactly who was on duty?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we can say exactly who the operations duty officer was and who was responsible for collating these reports or putting them into one report?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about operations centres. You worked in the Operations Centre in the course of 1994 and 1995, and you know where these reports were sent, when we say "superior command." A moment ago, you said that the reports were sent to the superior command, to the General Staff. This is my question: Do you know of the existence of the command post of the General Staff in Sarajevo, that's to say the Command in Sarajevo; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, there was a Supreme Command Staff at the Kakanj command post; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There was a command post at Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, when you say, "We submitted documents to the superior command, to the Supreme Command Staff," would you please tell the Trial Chamber where the 3rd Corps forwarded these reports? I'm thinking here of the regular daily combat reports and interim reports.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Both of those reports, the regular and the interim ones, we would be sending to the Staff in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, for a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, perhaps I made a mistake. I'm talking about the period after the Supreme Command Staff in Kakanj was established. I'm not talking about throughout the whole war. I'm talking about the period from 1995. I'm talking about the period of 1995.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't know about a specific time. For example, during the Farz operation, I was not the duty operations officer, so I don't know who the reports were sent to. There were --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you some documents regarding this operations logbook, so we will come to that. Before that, I just want to ask you this: You told us earlier that the operations logbook was supposed to have been kept in accordance with specific instructions, and we saw those instructions; is that correct? And you can see that the instructions were given by the chief of Staff, General Jusuf Khadr [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the paper we saw was not signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what actually was that operations logbook? Would you agree that that was a document of record?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The operations logbook was a document that mostly described -- that described what was going on at the Zenica Command Centre. The operations officer would enter into the logbook the main events, what he felt needed to be entered into the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you the following: It is correct, isn't it, that operations logbooks were not examined by the corps commander or the chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, it was looked at only by the duty officers, those who were relieving each other in the shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the duty operations officer would assess which information of those that were entered would be conveyed to the commander or the corps commander, the chief?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, if something was important and he felt that the chief of Staff or the commander needed to know that, then he would go to their cabinet and inform them about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move to the documents that I mentioned that I wanted to show to you before, I want to ask you something else that has to do something with the forward command posts of the 3rd Corps. It's correct, isn't it, that they were formed for specific assignments of shorter or longer duration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For example, there was a command post Orahovo; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Orahovo was formed for activities that had to do with the Sarajevo operation or the attempt to deblockade Sarajevo in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that this operation was -- bore the code signal "T"; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kamenica-Luke, the forward command post, was formed for the Farz operation specifically; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to clarify some codes or call signs that appear in documents, because these documents come from the Operations Centre. Mr. Sivro, the abbreviation used "OKM" means the basic command post, osnovno komandno mjesto; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: KM, K-M, means command post, istureno komandno mjesto?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In connection with these numerous forward command posts that you mentioned before and we added this one from July 1995, the one in Orahovo, would you agree for each of these command posts people had to be secured? I'm thinking about the officers and soldiers, in order for these command posts to be able to function?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You needed communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, communications, logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Documentation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell Their Honours how many of you were in the Operations Centre, operatives, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Which period are you thinking of, during the Farz operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the July-October 1995 period.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: There were very few at the Zenica command post. I was up there at the IKM. Pesto was at the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how many operatives were there in total, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "very few."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were very few of us during the operation, any given operation, at the command post. Mostly, I was in the field. I was not at the Operations Centre. Pesto was in the centre, and everybody else was out in the field. One from combat training would remain behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
