utterances.text: The gist of my question is this: The Operations Centre had very few people in order to cover such a number of forward command posts and command posts; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Yes, you are. The Operations Centre only had two officers, the chief and the desk officer. In this case, it was Pesto.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I want to ask you this: Do you agree, then, that it was very difficult to check any information? Did you check at all anything once you wrote it down, whatever you received?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: If it was of significance, then it would be checked. Depends on the importance of the information. Regular operations reports that we received from the units would be important. That would be the basis for us to draft our own reports. The reports that came from the units, we would look at them, we would see what that was about, and then we would draft our own reports. If anyone were to ask, for example, something for logistics, then we, as the duty officers, would convey that to the morale or the logistics section. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I want to ask you this: When you received the information from the subordinate unit, would you check its accuracy or would you just simply copy it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: We had to write it down, copy it into the operations report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would write it in, but you didn't check it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. I want to ask you this: If the operations logbook of the 3rd Corps contained the following, connections checked with everyone, with all units, meaning communications were checked, am I correct if I believe that actually communications were checked with the first subordinate unit with those who were directly connected to the Corps Commander at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: As duty operations officer, it was our assignment to check the units, to have all the subordinate units report back to us; not all of us, but this would be throughout the day, maybe at 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning, if we were at the command -- at the forward command post. If an operation was underway, then the commander there would do that, check the connections with the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first subordinate units to you, for example, divisions.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: For example, yes, if something was wrong, I would call the operations group, or actually it was already the division, the 35th Division, "Is everything all right, are the communication functioning," and that's what I would do. I didn't call the 318th, the 320th and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you very much. That is the gist of my question. Now, when you mentioned field telephones, induction telephones, you remember during these operations, it's correct, isn't it, that in August 1995 there was a shortage of cables and other spare parts? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically for August, but let's say at the start of the offensive or, actually, at the beginning of the operations, I recall that there was a shortage of induction telephones because that was something that was mentioned in the briefing by the communications or the signals chief, but I don't recall everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Your Honours, I would like the witness to look at document P2453 now. For the transcript, that is the monthly analysis of the 3rd Corps for August 1995. Can we please have the witness look at page 10 of the document. Actually, that is page 14 of the English version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to look where it talks about problems. Can you look at that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, it's above the heading, in the English version, the heading "Deployment," just above that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look? It says the problem, lack of PTK cable, manual UHF stations, spare parts for repair of radio equipment, because a quick way to repair materiel and technical equipment has not been solved, so MTS is material and equipment. Do you recall anything about this, Mr. Sivro? If you don't --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Your Honours, can this document be marked for identification? I'm not going to spend more time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the information we spoke about a moment ago. You said that you received information from subordinate units, and I'm referring to the information that is subsequently entered into the operations diaries, and then if somebody reported to you on something at a later date, you would include that information, too?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your own assessments, you would draft a report for your own commander and superior command; in other words, you were in a position to assess which information to include?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that was the information that we wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You received reports from all subordinate units of the 3rd Corps on a regular basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically about the El Mujahedin Detachment. You were located in the Operations Centre. This is my question: Did you ever take in your hands a report sent directly to the 3rd Corps from the El Mujahedin Detachment in the period while you worked in this Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I never received a report from them, either when I was in the Operations Centre or at the IKM. They placed a telephone call -- they placed a call two or three times, I don't know what it was about, but I made note of it. In other words, I never received a report from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to how they introduced themselves to you later on. Did you ever receive such reports from any other units of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, from those who were in direct communication with the 3rd Corps, we did. Sometimes it so happened that we wouldn't receive a report, but normally we received regularly these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was almost on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, please look again at the document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor today. That's P518. That's Exhibit P518. Mr. Sivro, you saw this logbook, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you testified about this logbook, when you were being proofed for this testimony, did you have a good look at this book?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, yes. This book is more or less well known to me. Sometimes I signed something that concerned me, but otherwise it concerned the headquarters administration. I didn't have much business to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the gist of my question: The dispatch book is a document of the headquarters administration, and you didn't have any dealings with it, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No. I would receive a report once every one or two months or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, in principle, that all types of documents such as this one had to be certified before they are logged, and I mean certify with a stamp.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Every document, we used to refer to logbooks such as this one as documents, had to contain an instruction at the very beginning, the number of pages, and then at the end of that logbook the accuracy of this document would be certified with the chief of -- by the chief of Staff with a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it would be certified thus?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 of this document. Look at this. It says "the new bridge Seliste." Does this mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We want the Trial Chamber to see the next page, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a place name, is it not? Can you make any inferences from this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we turn to page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, look at this. On the face of it, does this document indicate that it is a document of the 3rd Corps? Did you see any references to the 3rd Corps or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, there's nothing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, look at the columns in this log. Your Honours, I wish to make a correction for the record. Can the witness please read the columns out, since they were not properly translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, can you please read for the Bench what the headings of these columns are? The first one is date. Can you read them through, one by one?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "Date of receipt and delivery," "Type of mail -- reference number, type of mail," "sender," "receiver," and the signature of the receiver.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read column number 3 once more, slowly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "Type of dispatch." It says here, as far as I can see, "Sum."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Sum"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: That's at least how I read it, yes. A monetary amount, a sum.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, it seems that the interpreters don't understand. Can you -- will you agree if I read? "Type of package" or "shipment," and beneath it, it says "Monetary amount"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the gist of my question, and I didn't see that in the record. Next follows some columns and figures. Please, let's look at something which wasn't translated into English. In the top right-hand corner, do you see -- agree that it says "Form KP-6"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged, please? "Form KP-6".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, may this translation be corrected?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, let me ask you this: Do you agree that it is common knowledge, if you know, that the KP-6 form is a purely financial document, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about a KP-6 being a financial form.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you agree that this type of document is not the type of dispatch logbook normally produced by the 3rd Corps? Why would it contain this reference to a monetary amount, and can you tell us what this book is about? Can you state whether it is a 3rd Corps logbook?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the receiver can I conclude that, because there I see that 3rd Corps units are listed, and it's only on that basis that I could conclude that it is of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you did not have any dealings with this type of --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, no. With this type of dispatch log, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of the dispatch logbook. Mr. Sivro, can you please speak more slowly and clearly, because not everything you say is being recorded. You said to us a moment ago that the logbooks of outgoing mail and incoming mail had to bear a stamp, had to be certified by a stamp and had to be signed at the end; this is something you told us, right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If they are filled out to the full, they always had to contain the exact number of pages. The person keeping the records had to note down how many pages the logbook had in order to avoid any additional pages being added to it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, in the beginning the book had to say how many pages it had, and at the end you had to have the stamp of the Staff or whoever was the one keeping the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we look at page 21 in the B/C/S and page 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that judging by what we see, one would conclude that this is where the document ends; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is where it should end.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, may we turn to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document isn't certified at all?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, if this is the last page, then it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it does not contain the total number of pages, either?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, because it would normally have the page number in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions in relation to this document. If we could remove it, please. I want the witness to be shown MFI 519. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to remind you that you testified about this logbook of the 3rd Corps IKM today.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be removed now. I want the witness to be shown document D439. I want to explain to you that this is a set of documents. Due to the fact that we picked out only relevant pages for the Defence and the operations diary that the Prosecution wanted to have admit, it was not translated fully. This was why we had to prepare an exhibit differently. At this time, Your Honours, in order for you to be able to follow my examination, I believe it best to distribute copies of this document. Otherwise, it will be quite difficult to follow my questions. Can copies please be distributed to the witness, the Bench and learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please commit to your memory this strictly-confidential number that you see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which strictly-confidential number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the corner of the Bosnian version, the upper right-hand corner, it says: "Strictly confidential 02/3-1-381" and you have it in the upper right-hand corner of the English version, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right in believing that this strictly-confidential number relates to the IKM logbook and that subsequent numbers registered in the logbook would follow up on this one; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this number. Yes, that one. This is the number of this particular logbook, is it not? These are numbers that the documents in this logbook are given, or rather it is on the basis of this number that the documents referenced in the logbook are numbered, it's just another digit that is added to this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what we talked about a moment ago when you said that documents were sent to the General Staff. I want you to turn to page 5 of the Bosnian version, which is page 3 of the English version, Your Honours. This is an excerpt from the 3rd Corps IKM logbook, entry for the 15th of September. Can you please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Which page, page 5?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 5. Let me just observe that it was copied in such a way that the page was split. Look at the entry for the 15th of September, please. I'm speaking about the portion in the last column, where it says: "Regular BI GS ABH," that's to say the General Staff of the BH Army, and then IKM of the 3rd Corps, and then "A/A"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at the previous. Can you please find -- can you look at the previous page to see which logbook number was given to this entry. And you will -- previous page, Mr. Sivro, number 313; is that correct? Would you agree that this number, 313 --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So 313 refers to the entry of the 15th of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see that it says the General Staff of the BH Army, it doesn't say "Sarajevo." It doesn't say "Sarajevo" or "Kakanj" here in this column that you were looking at before.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, "BH Army" and" OKM of the 3rd Corps." It does not say "Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which column are you referring to, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm thinking of the last column in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Column number 10?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you this: Do you agree that this number, 313, must be added to the number that we had on the cover page, and that is how we get the number of the document; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at page 6 of this set of documents, Mr. Sivro, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we leave this page, I just want to understand what the title "Designation" in column 10 is supposed to mean. Do we designate the recipient of the document or the -- what's being designated there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you are right. It's designated -- actually, the person the witness is -- the person the document is being sent to or the person that receives it. I'm sorry, I thought we were talking about the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is dispatched to the units that are entered here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Main Staff at OKM 3K basic command post. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the forward command post but the basic command post in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, basic command post, and then also sent to archive. But we must also make a note that Zenica is not mentioned in that column.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main command post was in Zenica, so mostly those who wrote it would not write down "Zenica." It was known which command post -- or the basic command post was at Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just read what Their Honours are asking you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 6 of this set of documents. Your Honours, that is page 4 of the English version. Do you see that, Mr. Sivro? You can see it here and you can also have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it's a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please zoom in on the top part in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I am now asking you to look at the following. Do you agree that this is a document of the 3rd Corps, from most probably -- you mentioned the paragraphs earlier -- as the forward command post. I'm now just asking you to look at this number of this document, and do you agree -- look at the number on the operations logbook, in the notebook. This number, 313, that this corresponds to this number that we saw for the 15th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Strictly-confidential number 02/3-1-381-313. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that that is the number of the document that has been entered for the 15th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, and it was sent from the forward command post of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at to whom the document was sent to. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It was sent to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kakanj, the basic command post of the 3rd Corps, for their information, and the forward command post of the 2nd Corps, Kuburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now do you agree -- so earlier you saw that in the operations logbook -- can you please now look again at the entry for the 15th of September so you can compare that. Your Honours, you also have that on page 3 of the English version. And can you please look at page 5 again, and I'm just, please, asking you to compare what it says in the logbook and to look at and see what is written in the document. Do you agree that it just says the General Staff of the army, and the person who would open the logbook would not know whether it was sent to Sarajevo or to Kakanj, am I correct, according to your operations logbook?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: This is the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So according to the logbook, you would not see where the document had gone to; do you agree? It says "The General Staff," and you before told us that this was Sarajevo. But can you see that the document actually went to Kakanj, please?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, all right. Whoever was doing the entries in the logbook was not doing that job properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I wanted that. Can you look at something else? Do you agree that the document was also sent to the IKM of the 2nd Corps of Kuburic and that this was not entered in the logbook at all?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't written, and I repeat, the person who was making the entries of the logbook from the IKM of the 3rd Corps was not doing their job correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And now, Your Honours, if the witness can look at page 10 of this set of documents. This is page 10 of the English version also. And you have it here. You can see the entry before last, and it's on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We see the same thing, the General Staff of the Army of the BiH, OKM of the 3rd Corps, GLOC-Visoko, and a slash, a regular combat report. You could see that's how that entry was made; is that correct, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to just look at the previous page of the Bosnian version, and that is still page 10 of the English version, Your Honours. I just want you to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that for this date, the number 326 was entered, 327?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, 327 is entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And now, please, number 327, can you please check, it refers to strictly confidential for the 16th of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this number, strictly confidential, would need to have the number 02/3-1-381/327, this number that is added here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to look at page 11 of this set of documents. This is page 11 in the English version, Your Honours. The document has the title. Can you please look at that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "Regular Combat Report."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you can see the number can be seen clearly here?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: "327", the last number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that is the number we earlier found in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that there it just said "Sent to the General Staff," and if you look here, would you agree that the document was again sent to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, KM Kakanj, and can you please look at the other addressees of this document? And particularly pay attention here to this third thing. It says: "Sent to the GLOC at Visoko, to Halid Cengic personally"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please look at the previous page?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Regular combat report sent to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, main -- or basic command post of the 3rd Corps, GLOC-Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I ask you not to shout at me. I am doing my job here. I'm sorry, Witness and Your Honours. I would ask you, Witness, now to look at this. So this document has been sent to the GLOC-Visoko, to Halid Cengic personally. Would you agree that this, to Mr. Halid Cengic personally, is not something that is mentioned, do you agree, in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, it is not mentioned in the logbook of the IKM of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that these logbooks actually do not provide a precise picture or that they give imprecise information about where the documents are actually dispatched, do you agree, on the basis of what we have seen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: On the basis of what we have seen, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they missed the delivery to IKM 1, Kuburic, then the name of the person that it is being sent to in the GLOC-Visoko. And, Your Honours, we here have a series of documents, but there is no need. I think if you believe that it is necessary, I can demonstrate each document of the General Staff that is included in this document refers to Kakanj. I think that I have demonstrated sufficiently, and these documents here are a part of this exhibit. But if you believe, I can continue to elaborate, because this is very important for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please don't give closing argument, Madam Vidovic. Just carry on, do what you have to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I just wanted to cut things short. Perhaps the demonstration of these kind of documents -- the demonstration of these type of documents. But, all right, very well, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you look at page 15 of this document, or, rather, page 16 of this document or of this set of documents, or rather page 15. I apologise. Page 15. And, Your Honours, that is on page 16 of the English version. Can you look at that again, please?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This last entry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Regular combat report dispatched to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, GLOC is the basic command post of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to look at page 14 of the Bosnian version of the set of documents. Your Honours, that is page 16 of the English version. I would like to ask you to remember this number. Do you agree that the reference number is 549 for the 2nd of October?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Therefore, this document of the 2nd of October, 1995, would have the number strictly confidential 02/3-1-381/549; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to look at again page 16 of this set of documents. And that is page 17, Your Honours, of the English version. And if we can look at the front part of the document, if we can zoom in on that part. Can you see, Mr. Sivro, this number here 02/3-1-381/549 of the 2nd of October; do you agree that that is that number? It has 549 that you saw earlier in the logbook, and please can you check once again?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I checked. Yes, that is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please now look at where this document was delivered?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: In the logbook, it says it was sent to the General Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, GLOC main command post of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who is it dispatched to here?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: It's dispatched to the General Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kakanj, for information purposes of the 3rd Corps and the forward command post of the 2nd Corps, Kuburic, the Command of the 7th Corps, GLOC-Visoko, personally to Mr. Alija Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree again that this document or this logbook gives imprecise and unreliable information to whom exactly the documents were delivered?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The date is incorrect, it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you very much. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, your hour seems to be up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I don't have many more questions, but I really believe that it's important for the witness here to clarify. So if I can be given a little bit more time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I would now like the witness to look at document D441. Your Honours, I apologise. I have decided to cut short my questioning even more. Can we please look at MFI 511. MFI 511.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be, please, removed now? Can the witness be shown D444, entitled "Operations Diary." Your Honours, we made excerpts from the diary because of incomplete translation. Only small portions of this document were, in fact, translated as PT. I will ask that hard copies of the document be distributed again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While this is being handed down, I will ask you the following, Mr. Sivro, to save time: You said that you kept the operations diary in the month of September of 1995; is that right? You recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Before you started testifying here, or rather during proofing, did you have a good look at this document from the beginning to the end?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, not from the beginning to the end. Only to the part that concerned me. I only looked at the parts that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please look at page 3 of the document now. This is page 2 of the English version, Your Honours. Can you please confirm for us that the starting date of this diary, with number 1, starts on the 26th of August, 1995; is that right? Am I right, Mr. Sivro? Please have a look.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the bottom of the page, too. We can always see who handed the duty shift over and to whom, who received the duty shift at the end of each day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the penultimate page of the document, which is page 34 of the Bosnian version and page 3 of the English version, Your Honours. Do you agree that the last entry here is number 560; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the following page. Your Honours, perhaps this should be a good moment to make a break. I will not have too many questions after the break. The witness says that it would be good to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll give you a break, sir. We'll take a break for 30 minutes and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we left off dealing with this document that you have before you, the excerpt from the operations log. We stopped at page 34 in the Bosnian version, which was page 3 of the English version. You saw and said that the last number was -- the last number of the entry was 560. Please turn to the following page, that's to say page 35 of the Bosnian version. Your Honours, that's page 4 of the English version. Please look at what the document says. Can you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says that this notebook has 95 sheets, and this is certified by Colonel Ribo; do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. This was the chief of Department for Operations and Training, Colonel Haso Ribo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the number of the book is 35, the reference number; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is something you discussed when testifying about different types of logbooks and diaries, where you said that this type of document had to have this certification and the sum total of pages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. I said that both at the beginning of the logbook and at the end, it had to state the number of pages in total and there had to be the name of the person certifying this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, I asked my learned friend from the OTP to bring over an original. I believe you have the original of this document now with you. Can you please have a look at it. I'm asking my learned friends to confirm whether this is indeed the document that the witness has before him now. Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Sivro, have a look at this. Do you agree that the document states that there are 95 sheets, it says, that's pages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Ninety-five sheets.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you check and see how many sheets the document has? I managed to count 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've asked that question, Madam Vidovic, and the witness said, "Yes, this has the chief of -- this was the chief of Department for Operation and Training, Colonel Haso Ribo." At page 69, line 19: "Do you agree that it says that this notebook has 95 sheets and this is certified by Colonel Ribo; do you recognise this person?"

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ninety-five pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. You said "95 sheets" there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'm saying you're asking the same question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not. I'm asking the witness to double-check the number of pages and see how many sheets there are, in fact. I did the checking, but I'd like the witness to check that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you were not asking to double-check, because at line 13, page 70, you say: "Mr. Sivro, have a look at this. Do you agree that the document states that there are 95 sheets?" That's when I interrupted you. You were not saying, "Can you double-check?" Okay. If you're double-checking, double-check, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps this was not included in the interpretation you received, but this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you understand my request of you to check the number of pages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes. This book was finished at one point, and it should have been written that it was ended there. We can see that some pages were torn, and in fact it does not have as many pages as is stated here, it doesn't have 95 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, pages are missing?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Pages 19 to 91 are missing. These were probably blank pages that were torn off by someone. Perhaps they needed the paper. But at any rate, they should not have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you believe happened, but in fact you don't know what happened to the missing pages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic, if I may interrupt. Sir, you say pages 90 to 91 are missing, but in the copies that we are given, I do have 90 and 91.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is looking at the original of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us once more, for the sake of the transcript, which pages in the original -- from which page to which page are missing?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: There is page 19, and after page 19 --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: After page 19, the pages are missing until page 91. These were blank pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that where the entries in the diary end, this is where it should be stated that the book ends there; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what happened to the missing parts of it, you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the reason why I opposed the admission of this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem with what has been going on right now, and I would like you to please clear me. Mr. Witness, is the first page of this document not a cover page like that? I'm sorry. That's what I have. Can we put this cover page on the screen, please. Right. Isn't that the beginning of the book, the cover page of the book from the beginning, sir? Look at your monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the start of the operations logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Now, can you read the number of that page, please. No, no. Look at the screen, sir, and read the number of that page. 01855061. It starts at page 61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say that pages 19 and some other number are missing, I don't understand you, because it doesn't seem to me like page 19 would be part of this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. The witness has the original version in front of him. All of us have a photocopy. And the witness is referring to the pages as seen in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I understand that. All I'm saying is this page 61 is a cover page of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: ... and that is the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm still trying to talk to Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there are two types of numbers on this book. I would like to know which numbers are you talking about. There is the number that I've just referred you to, 01855061. There is the number in our photocopy, the second page after the cover page. It's a page which I think you testified to and said was instructions, and it was drafted by you. The third page, there is a 1 that's written by hand. Now, I don't know when you say page 19, are you starting from this one or are you starting from this 61? I would like you to tell us what is it -- which numbers are you talking about here before I carry on with my questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm talking about the operations logbook or diary, which was certified by the chief of Staff for Operations and Training, and I'm referring to the numbers of the pages contained in this notebook. The document was kept from page 1, which was handwritten, to page 17 and 18, which are there, and then the pages up to 91 are missing, they are blank. We probably relocated to a different IKM. I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say pages after 18, pages up to 91 are missing, they are blank. Now, which is which; are they missing or are they blank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are blank. This diary is complete, it's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So those pages are there, but they are not written on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are blank, but they are missing here. This operations logbook was finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. You see, why do we conduct a trial with books that are not the same? We should have here what he has there. If we don't have that, then I can't accept this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is why I wanted to look at the original. If I can assist by putting a question to the witness, and perhaps I can clarify this situation and assist by asking a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, when you count the blank pages that exist there, are there a total of 95?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: If the pages were there, there would be 95.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking are there, are those pages there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, they are not. They are missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Your Honours can also look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, in connection with this one last question, is it not allowed, in this type of document, to have blank pages before certification because anyone can then enter whatever they want into such a book?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: That's how it should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, very well. Your Honours, I just have one small group of questions now, if I may proceed. Can the witness at this point look at D442, please. D442.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, what are we supposed to do with D444?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have the document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: D444 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, before we get the document, I just want to put two questions like this to you, please: We have the operations diary and we have the war diary. Both of these documents are documents with -- documents of record?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If one and the same event is recorded in the war diary and in the operations diary, it would have to contain the same information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: If it's recorded and if the information is all right, then, yes, it would have to be like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if it's one event that happened at one point in time and it's the same, it has to be presented in the same way both in the war and the operations diary; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to ask you, please, to look at this document. First of all, it contains an excerpt from the operations diary for the 26th of the 19th, or actually for the 26th of September, at 1810 hours, and I would like you at this point in time to look at a note from the operations diary bearing the number 433 and 433 for the 26th of September. That is the second page of the Bosnian and the English version. Second page, please. I would like to draw your attention here, Witness, please, to this event that occurred at 1810 hours under number 433. Can you see that it says "1810 hours," the 26th of September is the date, and it says -- can you please follow the data carefully, and it says: "Major Enes Dolic reported that two Chetnik rocket projectiles were fired around 1800 hours from the villages Radnja-Vitkovci in the direction of Zenica, and then at 1820 hours the commander of the 3rd Corps ordered that three artillery projectiles be fired on the town of Doboj due to the firing of Chetnik rockets on Zenica". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we please have you remember this information and now I would like to ask you to look at page 3 of the document. This time, it's an excerpt from the war diary. This was the operations diary, and now here comes the excerpt from the war diary of the 3rd Corps Command, which also is marked with "F," and that would indicate "Farz"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 4 of the document, page 4 of the document. Can you please look -- the English version is all right, too. And can you please look at the bottom of the page. You will see, around 1810, can you see, it says: "Around 1810 Major Enes Dolic informed that two projectiles were fired around 1800 hours from the Chetnik military positions in the direction of Zenica." Do you recognise this information, this information of the 26th of September at 1810 hours? Do you see that, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And now it says: "Due to the mentioned activity of the aggressor, the commander of the 3rd Corps issued an order to fire three Howitzer shells on the command post of the Operative Group Doboj." And now, please, I would like to ask you the following: Do you agree that both of these documents, both of these excerpts, excerpts one from the operations diary and the second from the war diary, talk about the call of Major Enes Dolic and the order of the commander of the 3rd Corps, Mahmuljin at 1810 hours? Please, do you agree that here in the first it says that two projectiles were fired in the direction of Zenica, and that here in this last part an order was made to fire a military target, the command post of the Operations Group Doboj?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, according to the operations diary, you saw that it said fire three projectiles from artillery weapons on the town of Doboj; do you understand the difference, Mr. Sivro? You're a soldier.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I understand the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The operations diary was probably -- the entry was made by the duty officer, and the war diary was written by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By somebody less educated or trained?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Well, the person who wrote into the war diary is more trained, because he wrote that military targets were being fired at.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the explanation. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. Now, please, do you now understand these two documents as indicating, isn't it, a different, completely different essence? In one, the commander of the 3rd Corps orders an attack on a legitimate target, the commander of an operations group, and in the second one it says fire on the town of Doboj. Please, is that the same?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: No, it's not the same. This major here did not understand the order of the commander and the person who recorded the entry in the war diary probably spoke with the commander and he knew what the commander meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you then agree that one very crucial fact here would indicate that the corps commander could be sent to prison for firing on the town of Doboj. Do you understand that this type of document is such that the reliability of the facts cannot be established on the basis of the entries here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you're asked to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your last answer, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I agree. I agree that information that individual duty officers, especially those who did not have any particular experience, did not make the entries in the way that it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, can this document please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Any re-examination, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could just have a second to get the podium up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, sorry, before the Prosecution starts, can I just follow up on one little question relating to your last question to the witness. Just exactly where was the aggressor's command post located? Was it in Doboj town or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command post of the operations group of Doboj, as far as I know, was in Doboj. It was in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was in Doboj. But, Your Honours, if you permit me just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's not the same to issue an order to fire at the Command of the operations group and to fire at the town of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Of course, it's not logical to issue an order to fire at the town of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that we have two different pieces of information on the same event? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know one thing. Doboj, was the city of Doboj attacked, together with its civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were attacked from the town of Doboj. We, when I say "we," I mean the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as far as defence operation is concerned, did you attack only the enemy, the militaries, or did you respond by also attacking the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina never attacked civilians, only military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would ask -- we had marked Exhibit PT2463 as being marked for identification. I would ask that that be tendered into evidence at this point. I think I had laid a foundation for the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: PT?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was PT -- P02463. It had been marked for identification as 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was 2463, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it was marked for identification as what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, am I correct if I assume that this is the most recent document that we discussed, that the witness looked at? Your Honours, I would like it for the transcript to record that I oppose the introduction of this document. I dispute the authenticity of the document, because the witness has already finished, and that the Prosecution did not establish a sufficient basis for the document to be admitted into the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I marked that -- I marked this document for identification as a courtesy to the Defence. I certainly felt that at the time that I had the foundation to admit the document, so I certainly do think it is an appropriate time for the document to be admitted. In terms of the authenticity of the document, I was listening very carefully during the course of Madam Vidovic's cross-examination, and I don't think her cross-examination touched upon the contents of the document certainly as it exists in -- as an exhibit in this case. Whether there were pages missing or not, certainly that's not -- we wouldn't use the fact that there were pages missing to prove a point. We were using the contents of the document, what was in the document and what was shown to the witness to make our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, perhaps not today but during final arguments, the parties to give guidance to this Court as to what to do with documents that are marked for identification, are used for leading, are used for cross-examination, and then we are supposed not to admit them. I just don't know. It's a very strange procedure, this. A document that is not being admitted should not be discussed on the transcript. It should be stopped from word "go" and be thrown out completely. Now, I want to know, what are we going to do with that part of the transcript, Madam Vidovic, that you used to attack this document if this document is not part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think and the practice that I have had so far, is that that part of the transcript by any means does remain. Simply, the document is not admitted. This is according to the practice that I have followed so far on this Tribunal. The document is not admitted unless the party that -- unless the party that is asking for it to be admitted has not provided sufficient arguments or the other side is more persuasive, but the transcript remains. At least that was the practice in the case before this Tribunal that I was involved in before. That is the practice that was followed by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question, then, is: What impact does that transcript have on the case? Because my understanding of not admitting a document or an exhibit is that it is not here, we haven't spoken about it, its existence is not reflected on the transcript. Now, you have cross-examined, you have lead all this information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. And I'm just asking for guidance. What do we then do with that part of the transcript when the document is not there for us to say -- to make a determination at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, it is my position that the transcript should reflect precisely what happened in the courtroom. It should be evident that the party, either the Prosecution or the Defence, attempted to have the document admitted, that contrary arguments were given, and the Chamber simply decided this or that. But I think that the transcript remains intact and that that should not -- and this should not have any effect on the transcript. The transcript should reflect the entire discussion that took place before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, do you have anything to contribute on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: We concur, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: We concur, Your Honour, with Madam Vidovic's position on the record and whether the -- whether exhibits not admitted into evidence should be -- whether the portion of the record that relates to that exhibit should be -- should remain on the record, we concur with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have a problem. We marked for identification document 511, and you're asking for its admission. It is a copy of the original which we saw during the cross-examination. That's what it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, during the cross-examination, Defence asked for the admission of the original. No? Is it what you did? Thank you. But in any case, we are now discussing whether to admit a copy of the original document and not the original document itself. So on the transcript, you are contesting the authenticity -- challenging the authenticity of the document because there's no certification at the end of the document. That is on the transcript. Thank you, I think I got the explanations. I was a bit confused, but now everything is straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I may just interject on this one point concerning the issue of whether the original or the electronic version goes into evidence if the Chamber decides to admit what's been marked as P -- or what's been marked as 511 for identification. When the Office of the Prosecution seized original logbooks from the archives of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, assurances were given that those original logbooks would be returned to those archives. I would respectfully ask that the electronic version be substituted for the original so that at the completion of this case, to include the appeal, those original materials may be returned to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If they were to remain as part of the evidence, they would remain with the Registry for an indefinite period of time, perhaps to be archived with the material from this Tribunal, in which case they would not be returned to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the agreement that was reached when we took the original hard copies of these logbooks. So that's my limited submission. It's clear from the record and the fact that Your Honours have looked at this logbook, that there are pages missing, and we would strongly suggest that the electronic version be substituted for the original, which is a chain-of-custody document, needs to go back into the evidence vault, and ultimately, pursuant to the assurances given to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we would ask that that material go back to where it rightfully belongs, which is in the archives of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I could just say something briefly. You saw clearly that actually this copy does not correspond to the original. If a photocopy of the original is made and even if there are blank pages, then the page that states that this is an entire document needs to be copied and included in the copy of the document, and this is why, in the practice before this Tribunal, I had the following situation: A document was admitted like this, which had a blank page, and then suddenly at one point in the proceedings another copy of the document appeared, and that page that had previously been blanked was now filled in, and we had considerable problems because of that. What I want to say, Your Honours, is because of that, each document that is being admitted as a photocopy of the original, then it must be a photocopy of the original. In this case, it obviously is not. At the end, it says it has 90 pages. You saw for yourself that it does not have 90 pages, and then there are blank pages there. And that is why I do not believe that this actually is a photocopy of the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, your point is well taken, but there could be some sort of meaning to be elicited from the document. If you look at the last page of the photocopy, which appears to be the right side of page 16 or maybe the left side of page 16, there are two signatures after the entry number 560, down at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, yes, but you have that on each page. You can ask the witness about this, Your Honour. These are signatures which state duty shift handed over to and duty shift received by.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you help us with this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I've seen this. Under item 560, we have who took over the duty shift, and we also have who handed the duty shift over to that other person, and then it goes on like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand the witness correctly, actually, the logbook should have gone on, because there was someone who took over. My question was only related to the fact that these signatures might have implied -- that these signatures might have implied the closure of the logbook. But your view is that this is not the closure, that the logbook actually went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, could you explain something else? You told us something in passing. You said, "Unless we changed IKM." At one point in time, you said that this logbook had pages missing, and then you said, "if this is not correct, unless --" I wish I could find it in the transcript. You said "unless." Sir, could you please explain? Do you remember that you said that, you said "unless" at one point in time, "unless we change something"? Do you remember when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember that. This diary is closed. This means that the IKM was moved to a different location, and this logbook or diary was closed, although it was not done properly, because the person from the Operations Centre should have noted down that the entries in that logbook were finished with such-and-such an item, and then it should have been signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's a question of procedure that was not done correctly. Someone was incompetent along the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Witness, the issue is: How can you be so certain that the logbook was closed at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of the fact that there are no more entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But there could have been. I don't think we can pursue this matter much further. Let us deliberate on it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rule 89 of the Rules says a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The decision adopting guidelines on the admission and presentation of evidence and conduct of counsel in court has attached to each of those guidelines and paragraph (l) of those guidelines is headed "Tendering of Exhibits Through Witnesses." It says: "Where one of the parties seeks the admission of a document through a witness, it must demonstrate to the Trial Chamber the relation between the witness and the document. The Trial Chamber may not allow the admission through that particular witness of documents which lack such relation." I think the relation with this witness has been demonstrated. The document is admitted. May it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to clarify that that was the electronic version and not the original version of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. If we could have the document, the original version back, because we have to return it to the evidence vault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If I could add something. The B/C/S version, I think, of the Defence document is the same as the B/C/S version of our exhibit. However, we've translated certain portions into English that they haven't, and that's the difference between the two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you saying? The B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I believe Your Honours were discussing Exhibit -- I think Defence Exhibit 444 and -- or Court Exhibit 522 and the exhibit which I just tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we are doing that, but don't talk about that. Just carry on with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 518. 518. And if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and English. Excuse me, page 3 of the B/C/S and English. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, you see the document in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I was wondering, do you know where or how logbooks such as these would be acquired? And I'm speaking of the blank, before they were actually written into, where they were purchased.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I don't know. This was the job of the headquarters administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 521.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, do you remember this document? I believe you had spent some time discussing the contents of this document during the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if you could just look at the strictly confidential number and keep that in mind. Now if the witness could be shown the document marked as MFI 519. Mr. Sivro, would you agree that this document is the same as the one you just looked at?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The same, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that MFI 519 be tendered into evidence. And the reason I do that, in addition to the Defence exhibit which is already in evidence, is because obviously some of the translations that we have done, we have different pages translated than the Defence and their exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us clarify the following: What the Defence showed to the witness were portions, pages of this document, definitely not the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is a logbook, so essentially, I mean, though the specific entries may differ, the form in which it appears is very similar. Now, this witness spent a considerable amount of time discussing the form of the document, discussing specific entries in the document, and so certainly I think that a sufficient relation has been established between the witness and the document. Certainly, if he can discuss a particular entry which is -- which the Defence felt that he could discuss, then I think he can discuss any number of entries. And I'm not going through that with him in the interest of time, but I do think that through the Defence's cross-examination, a relation has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm not quite sure I'm following you. I must be confused here. You said in the beginning that you are tendering it, notwithstanding the fact that it is the same document as the one that was tendered by the Defence. Which one was tendered by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exhibit 521 is the Defence exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say it's the same thing as 519?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: 519, exactly. It's just that we've translated different excerpts than the Defence translated, but the document itself is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. It's not that it's not the same. We combined parts of the logbook with other documents, if you recall, with reports and so on and so forth. That's why the document isn't similar at all. It only contains some portions of this logbook. If you remember, I compared some documents which were indeed sent with the pages of the logbook, so we can't say that it's one and the same document. There must have been have been an error somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's not one and the same document, maybe then that's one of the reasons we should admit both of them, because they speak to different topics. Okay, the document is then admitted, and may it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one question. I don't know if this is complicated, but I would like you to be very clear. You've told us that you would receive reports stemming from all units, all subordinate units subordinate to the 3rd Corps. You've also told us that you personally, as far as your function goes, you had never seen a report from the El Mujahedin Detachment. I am not challenging this statement of yours, but I would just like to know, when you are referring to a certain period, I would like to know what period you're referring to. We are referring to 1994, you started -- rather, correction. We are not concerned by the year 1994, when you started working, but what we are interested in is 1995. Therefore, when we talk about 1995, the El Mujahedin Detachment, was it always subordinated to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SIVRO
utterances.text: The El Mujahedin Detachment, I don't know about that detachment. Never showed up -- nobody ever showed up from that detachment, as far as I was able to see in the 3rd Corps. I never saw those men. I only had contacts with them on two occasions, as the logbooks indicate, when a person called on their behalf. I never received any reports from this unit, and had I received any, there would have been a record of that somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Witness, but I would like to know if, by any chance, the detachment was subordinated to another unit.
